description: We’re a tech-focused team interested in AI, software, and building ambitious products. We’re looking for motivated people with strong development, design, or product skills who want to build fast, experiment, and create something impactful.
summary:
We built SFSS, an offline tool that turns NASA's microgravity combustion research into quick answers you can check against the source. In space, flames behave differently: without gravity there is no buoyant convection, so a fuel burns as a slow, spherical flame. This makes spacecraft fire safety hard to predict from experience on Earth.

SFSS does two things. First, it predicts how fast a fuel droplet burns in a given cabin atmosphere: oxygen, CO₂, helium, pressure, droplet size and fuel. The model is a machine-learning model we trained on 259 FLEX experiments from the International Space Station, with mean error 0.055 mm²/s and R² 0.65. Second, it answers questions using only 16 NASA technical reports, and every answer cites the report page it came from.

Anti-Fire is a desktop app built on SFSS with one screen for calculations, CSV import and questions to the reports. Any other program can connect through an HTTP API. Everything runs locally on a laptop without internet.

This gives engineers who choose atmospheres for spacecraft and lunar bases a quick way to compare options and a direct link to the evidence. It also makes decades of NASA experiments usable instead of buried in PDFs.
details:
SFSS (Space Fire Safety Service) runs offline on a laptop and does two things.

1. It predicts how fast a fuel droplet burns in a given cabin atmosphere (oxygen, CO₂, helium, pressure, droplet size, fuel). The model is a random forest trained on 259 FLEX experiments from the ISS (NASA report NTRS-20150023456): mean error 0.055 mm²/s, R² 0.65. It warns when the input is outside the training data.

2. It answers questions using only 16 NASA technical reports. A local Ministral 3B model writes the answer from the passages it found, and every answer cites the report and page.

On top of it we built:

- Anti-Fire, a desktop app for calculations, CSV import and questions to the reports.

- SFSS Playground: six habitat modules ranked by fire risk, a rotatable 3D view of each module with a spherical microgravity flame that grows and turns sooty as oxygen rises, and a "Next experiment" map that suggests which conditions to test next.

- A telemetry monitor that shows how other software can call SFSS through its API.

IMPACT

Engineers choosing atmospheres for spacecraft and lunar or Mars habitats can compare options in seconds and go straight to the source. Researchers see where data is missing. Students see why fire behaves differently in space.

TOOLS

Python, FastAPI, scikit-learn, pandas, NumPy, ONNX Runtime; TypeScript, React, Vite, Tauri, three.js/WebGL; LM Studio, Ollama, Ministral 3B, MiniLM; built on a MacBook with 8 GB of memory.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

Honesty about limits: the model covers fuel droplets, not burning materials, so it compares atmospheres rather than forecasting a fire; we publish its error and flag inputs outside the data. Privacy: nothing leaves the machine. Accessibility: macOS, Linux and Windows, English and Russian. Rules: open models only, no NASA logos.
